episodes.title: The AI Content System Behind 200M Views — Sarah Chieng, Cerebras & Cova Lee, OpenAI
episodes.description:
Sarah Chieng (head of developer experience at Cerebras) and Cova Lee (OpenAI developer experience, formerly a full-time creator) share the agent-powered system they use to make content. It runs across six stages: ideating, scripting, recording, editing, repurposing and publishing. Topics include swipe files and custom research tools, voice-based scripting and script skills, shot lists, design systems, and editing through APIs and computer use. They also cover cutting long videos into shorts, scheduled publishing, and a weekly skill that reviews your own process. Their main point: let AI take the tedious work so you can treat content as a craft, not make slop.

episodes.title: Does Code Quality Still Matter? It Depends on This — Max Kanat-Alexander, Capital One
episodes.description:
Every senior engineer's answer is "it depends." Max Kanat-Alexander says what it actually depends on. Code quality always existed for two things: understanding a system and safely changing it. AI is making a new kind of software common: disposable software, with low consequences, few dependents and near-zero cost to replace or maintain. For that software, quality doesn't matter. For durable software it matters more than ever. He also shows how to make systems more disposable and how to make rigor cheap through standards, in-workflow tooling, easy testing and maximum strictness.

episodes.title: One Day, $1,000 in Tokens: An AI War Room for Legacy Code — Ford Prior, GEICO
episodes.description:
At GEICO, coding got fast but everything around it (decisions, sign-offs, context) stayed slow. Ford Prior's fix was a multiplayer, AI-native war room: the right decision makers, one driver, and fleets of agents wired into GEICO's knowledge, tools and code. His bet was that one day and $1,000 in tokens could map a legacy claims domain end to end and ship one real change. He ran it three times across rentals, damages and salvage. He covers FleetKit, the markdown rulebook that steers the agent fleet, plus the worksheets and diagrams it produced and what he'd change next.

episodes.title: AI Cut Our Research Time From 7 Days to 15 Minutes — Gareth Yoder, Vanguard
episodes.description:
Gareth Yoder leads the cash program at Vanguard. He walks through modernizing a cash ledger that takes up to 30 million calls a day, running data, producer and consumer migrations in parallel. The turning point was exposing the legacy code base to AI tools through an MCP server. Research that took a mainframe engineer seven days dropped to 15 minutes. He closes with five lessons: make legacy code AI-queryable, treat migration docs as product, reimagine instead of lift-and-shift, adopt AI incrementally, and never skip observability.

episodes.title: Is a Faster Model Actually Faster? Test the Whole Job — Morgan Suo, MiniMax
episodes.description:
A faster model only helps if the finished job gets faster. Morgan Suo of MiniMax uses one real research task to test the changes inside the M3.1 Flash model: an analyst checking whether circuit-board suppliers are turning AI demand into cash. The changes are sparse attention on long inputs, a 4-bit KV cache, low-precision experts, speculative decoding, server load and reasoning budgets. Each one saves compute, and each can quietly cost accuracy or wait time. She then shows how to judge a model switch: check sources and calculations, count the full cost of a usable report, and make the result repeatable.

episodes.title: Same GPU, 50% More Output: Why the Operator Matters — Oliver Kennon, SemiAnalysis
episodes.description:
Buying GPUs gives you potential. The operator decides how much useful work you actually get out of them. Oliver Kennon looks at compute as a commodity market: on the same B200 chip, the serving stack alone can deliver about 50% more output. Cluster security is part of whether intelligence is "useful". SemiAnalysis's ClusterMAX rates operators, and rental price and production cost are different numbers. Your spot on the cost curve depends on your competitors, not just you. He closes on what it takes to build credible compute grades and futures.

episodes.title: A Bank Built Its Own Coding Agent. It Took Off — Felipe Felisola Caso & Francesco Galletta, Monzo
episodes.description:
Monzo's in-house agent started as an emoji you could react with in Slack. Now it authors over 10% of all merged PRs across Monzo's tech teams and runs more than 1,800 tasks a day. Felipe and Francesco explain why it worked so fast. Their answer is the "lots of little multipliers" Monzo already had: an MCP gateway into internal tools and knowledge, a sandboxed agent orchestration system built for a regulated bank, and a platform that turns the agent itself into a building block. That building block now handles incidents, on-call data quality and requests from non-engineers.

episodes.title: Shipping AI Into 5 Major Banks Without a 12-Month Compliance Wait — Al Chen, Cisco

He covers the build pipeline, CVE remediation with agents writing and testing exploits, backup and restore verification, PII leaking through LLM judges, and why zero leakage and data sovereignty are never free.

episodes.title: Why AI Agents Will Need Their Own Bank Accounts — Lincoln Murr, Coinbase
episodes.description:
Lincoln Murr, head of AI product at Coinbase, explains agentic finance: agents that pay with money and agents that grow it. He covers the path from AgentKit, an early experiment giving an AI a wallet, to x402, an open standard built on the long-unused HTTP 402 "payment required" code. x402 now handles hundreds of millions of agent transactions a month. Other topics are microtransactions as a replacement for the ad economy, agents running trades on simple instructions, and what two years of building taught Coinbase. Trust is earned step by step, and the AI is the enabler, not the product. He ends with a look at agents that can pay for their own upkeep.
